svg.title: A low sodium: the whole approach, in five numbered bands with the limit down the side
svg.desc: A low sodium: the whole approach. 1 Assess. How low? Below 125 is profound. How long? 48 hours or more, or unknown, is chronic. How symptomatic? 2 Act on the symptoms. A fork. On one side, severe: seizure, coma, persistent vomiting; and moderately severe: nausea, confusion, headache (a senior decision); both lead to 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes. Up to three. Stop at plus 5. On the other side, mild or none leads to: there is time. Find the cause first. Both rejoin. 3 Investigate. Serum osmolality: below 275, it is real. Urine osmolality: above 100, vasopressin is on. Urine sodium: 30 or below, or above 30. Diuretic or kidney disease? The bedside, last: dry, normal or overloaded. Exclude the glands before you write SIADH. 4 Why, and 5 Treat it. Urine osmolality 100 or below: too much water for the solute; stop what is contributing. Dry: diarrhoea, vomiting, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency; 0.9% saline, 0.5 to 1.0 mL/kg an hour. Overloaded: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; fluid restriction. Normal volume: SIADH; fluid restriction. Treat the driver. In every box: check the drugs and the drip. A rail from band 2 to the foot: no more than 10 in the first 24 hours, then 8 a day. At its foot, a telephone: past it? Stop, and ring.

text.tspan: No more than 10 in the first 24 hours,
A low sodium: the whole approach
check the drugs and the drip
